explain.say: An old sailor grabs a young man on his way to a wedding and will not let go. He holds him with his glittering eye, and the guest has to listen. That is how Coleridge's poem begins, the first poem in Lyrical Ballads in 1798. The panels tell the Mariner's tale.

explain.say: Look at panels two and three. An albatross leads the ship out of the Antarctic ice, and the sailors love it. Then the Mariner shoots it with his crossbow. The poem never says why. Why might Coleridge leave the reason out?

explain.say: See how one act spreads through the web. A polar spirit takes revenge, the wind dies and the sun burns: water, water, every where, nor any drop to drink. The crew hang the dead bird around his neck. A ghost ship comes, and all two hundred crew drop dead. Why is he the one left alive?

The fifth panel. Alone, he sees water snakes shining in the moonlight and blesses them, unaware. At that moment the albatross falls from his neck into the sea. Notice the ballad stanza: four lines, rhyme on lines two and four. What changed inside him?

explain.say: Two readings. On the left, a Christian allegory of sin and grace: he prayeth best, who loveth best all things both great and small. On the right, a crime against nature, and trauma that must be retold. Wonderful. Challenge: the guest wakes a sadder and a wiser man. Wiser about what?

left.title: Christian allegory
points: He prays best who loves best

faq.q: Why does the Mariner shoot the albatross?
faq.a: The poem gives no reason, which is the point. The act seems motiveless, an irrational crime against a creature that trusted the crew, and the rest of the poem works out its consequences.
asks: Why did he kill the albatross?

faq.a: Readings vary: a sign of grace or of Christ, the bond between humans and nature, or a burden of guilt, which is why we still say an albatross around your neck.
The Mariner looks at the water snakes and blesses them unaware, feeling love for living things. The albatross then falls from his neck, and his penance begins.
asks: When does the albatross fall off?

faq.q: Why must the Mariner keep telling his story?
faq.a: As part of his penance he feels an agony that forces him to retell his tale to certain people he meets, teaching them to love all creatures.
asks: Why does the Mariner stop the wedding guest?

faq.a: A four-line stanza that alternates lines of four and three beats, usually rhyming on the second and fourth lines. Coleridge uses it to echo old folk ballads.

facts: The poem opened Lyrical Ballads in 1798 and is divided into seven parts.
Coleridge added the prose gloss in the margins for the 1817 version in Sibylline Leaves.
The phrase an albatross around one's neck comes from this poem.
